prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: Fifteen, Before, For

outputs.L1:
Fifteen years later, the old tollbooth keeper remains at his post, yet—regrettably, his brains blown out—he can neither break a twenty nor offer the directions I have long forgotten. I did telephone ahead; what did you expect? Before I can so much as blink, I find myself parked before the unbelievably small, unlit house. My finger rests upon the buried bell—nothing. For hours I have wandered about, and I loathe to be the one to say it, but no one is home in Zanesville, Ohio.

My dusty toothbrush awaits me—of this I feel quite certain—and my teenage reflection lingers in the dust-dimmed mirror. Only now I fear I shall be compelled to disturb the slow, fine snowfall of dust that has descended, year upon year, upon my blanket and my hair; to don my dust-covered clothes; and to walk without a sound, trailing my eternal lunar footprints down the windless hall, and, at last, down the stairs.

It will not happen overnight. But one of these days I shall arrive; I shall go down to sit with the father—the elderly father, strictly speaking, of never truly having been there. I shall sit down and eat my bowl of dust, like all the rest.
outputs.L2:
A decade and a half has passed, and although the old man who tends the tollbooth remains in his usual spot, he sadly can't make change for a twenty—his head has been shot open—nor can he give me the directions I've lost. Did I call ahead? Of course I did, what did you expect? In no time at all I find myself stopped in front of the impossibly tiny house that sits there in darkness. My finger presses the bell that's sunk into the wall, but there's only silence. I've spent hour after hour wandering about, and it pains me to admit it to you, but nobody answers in Zanesville, Ohio.

I'm certain my dust-coated toothbrush still waits somewhere for me, and so does the reflection of my teenage self, faint in the mirror that grime has clouded. My worry now is that I'll have to stir up the delicate, gradual snowfall of dust that's been settling season after season across my hair and my blanket, that I'll have to dress myself in dust-blanketed garments, and move silently, leaving behind my everlasting moon-like tracks, along the still corridor and finally down the staircase. This won't come to pass anytime soon. Yet someday I'll get there; I'll descend to take a seat beside the father—the aged father, that is, of a person who was never truly present at all. I'll settle in and eat my bowl of dust, just as everyone else does.
outputs.L3:
**Return**

The old tollbooth keeper is still there, fifteen years later, seated at his post exactly as I remember him. But he is dead now—propped in his little booth like a mannequin, his hands stiff on the counter, unable to make change or point the way to anyone who stops. Cars idle before him, waiting for a gesture that will never come. I pass through anyway, out of habit, out of some strange loyalty to the ritual, and continue down the road that has always led here.

The house waits at the end of it, small and dark against the flat Ohio sky. Zanesville. I knock, and then I wait. Hours pass. No lamp flickers on behind the windows; no footstep answers from within. The house is empty, as it has perhaps always been empty, and I sit on the porch step in the failing light, telling myself that someone will come, that someone must come, though I know better.

I think of the things I left behind when I first went away. My toothbrush, surely still resting in its cup by the sink. My reflection, caught in the bathroom mirror, waiting patiently to greet a boy who never returned. I imagine all of it preserved beneath a soft gray shroud, the small artifacts of a childhood suspended in time, gathering the dust of years I spent elsewhere. Everything is exactly where I left it, and everything is buried.

That dust is the truest thing in the house. It has settled over the furniture, the photographs, the silence, marking the slow accumulation of the years the way rings mark the age of a tree. But it is more than time made visible. It is the residue of something that was never fully alive here—a family that was always more absence than presence, a home built around an emptiness at its center. The dust does not cover what once was warm; it reveals what was cold all along.

And yet I know I will come back. Not today, perhaps, and not soon—but inevitably. One day I will sit down beside my father in that dim, still house, and I will take my place in the long inheritance of our silence. This is the legacy he leaves me: not land, not name, not love, but absence itself—the quiet art of being gone while remaining, of waiting in a house where no one ever arrives. I will sit with him and share it, because it is mine now too, and there is nowhere else, finally, that I belong.
outputs.L4:
# The Return

The poem opens on the threshold of a house that has stood empty for fifteen years, and from its first lines it establishes an atmosphere thick with the residue of time. The speaker approaches the childhood home not with anticipation but with a quiet dread, as if he already suspects what he will find. The door, when it opens, releases not warmth or memory but a breath of stale air, and everywhere the eye settles there is dust—settled on windowsills, gathered in corners, filming the surfaces of forgotten objects. This dust becomes the poem's central and most insistent image, a soft gray shroud laid over everything that once held life.

Through careful accumulation of detail, the poem builds its portrait of decay. Paint peels from the walls in curling flakes; floorboards sag and complain underfoot; cobwebs stretch across doorways like the ropes that mark off ruins. What was once a home has become a hollow shell, and the imagery of abandonment works steadily to dramatize the enormous distance between the past the speaker carries in memory and the present he now stands within. Fifteen years have not merely aged the house—they have emptied it of meaning, transforming a place of belonging into a museum of absence.

At the heart of the speaker's return lies a longing that the poem gradually reveals to be impossible to satisfy. He has come back hoping, perhaps without admitting it to himself, to recover something: a feeling, a presence, a version of himself that once lived here. Most of all, the poem suggests, he has come seeking the father figure whose absence haunts these rooms. Yet each detail he encounters only deepens the recognition that there is nothing here to reclaim. The past cannot be entered again like a room; it has closed behind him permanently, and no amount of standing in the ruins can conjure back what time has carried away.

The poem's emotional and symbolic climax arrives in the image of eating "a bowl of dust." This startling gesture crystallizes the speaker's confrontation with futility. To eat the dust is to take absence itself into the body, to consume and internalize the very substance of loss rather than fight against it. It is an act of grim acceptance—a resignation that abandons the fantasy of recovery. In swallowing what remains, the speaker acknowledges that decay is now his only inheritance, that the nourishment he sought has been replaced by the ashes of what no longer exists.

What makes this final image so poignant is the deeper realization it carries: that perhaps home and the father were never truly present to begin with. The return has not simply revealed a loss that occurred over fifteen years—it has exposed a more painful truth, that the wholeness the speaker mourns may have been an illusion all along, a construction of longing rather than a memory of something real. The nostalgic journey backward, undertaken to recover the past, ends instead in the clear-eyed and sorrowful understanding that there was never anything solid to return to. The dust, in the end, is not only what time has left behind, but what was perhaps always there beneath the surface, waiting.

# Fifteen Minutes Before

There's something special about the fifteen minutes before an important moment. Whether it's a job interview, a first date, or a major presentation, those final moments carry a weight all their own.

I remember standing outside the conference room, watching the clock. Fifteen minutes remained before I would give the most important speech of my career. My hands trembled slightly, but I reminded myself that I had prepared thoroughly for this exact moment.

Time works differently in those quiet stretches. Before you know it, the anticipation builds into something almost tangible. Fifteen minutes can feel like an eternity, yet somehow they slip away far too quickly for comfort.

I used those precious minutes wisely. I reviewed my notes one final time, took several deep breaths, and reminded myself why I had worked so hard for this opportunity. Everything I had done—every late night, every rehearsal—had led to this point.

There's wisdom in the phrase "arrive fifteen minutes before." It gives you space to collect your thoughts, to settle your nerves, and to prepare mentally for whatever lies ahead. Those who rush in at the last second miss this valuable buffer.

When the door finally opened, I felt ready. The fifteen minutes before had transformed my anxiety into focus. I walked in with confidence, grateful for the time I had taken to prepare myself for success.

Sometimes the moments before an event matter just as much as the event itself. Use them well.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a surreal prose poem about returning to your childhood home after fifteen years to find it abandoned and covered in dust.
counterfactuals.output:
# The House That Kept Waiting

The key still fit, which was the first cruelty.

Fifteen years and the lock remembered me like an old grievance, turning over with a sigh. Inside, the air had gone thick as amber, and everything wore its coat of gray velvet—the piano, the banister, the photographs whose faces had surrendered their names to the dust.

I walked through rooms that had shrunk to fit a stranger's memory. My childhood bed, still made, held the impression of a smaller body, a ghost of the boy who slept there dreaming of escape. He got his wish. I am the proof of it, standing here in shoes too large for these hallways.

Dust fell like slow snow, like the sediment of hours. It had been falling since I left, I understood now—accumulating in my absence, one particle for every day I did not return. On the kitchen table, my mother's teacup waited half-full of nothing, its ring stained permanent as a wedding vow. The refrigerator hummed a note I'd forgotten I knew by heart.

*You took so long,* the walls whispered through their peeling wallpaper skin. *We rehearsed your return a thousand times.*

In the hallway mirror, dust had drawn a portrait of my father's face over mine, or maybe time had, or maybe they are the same artist working in the same medium of forgetting. I raised my hand. The reflection raised a hand older than I remembered choosing to become.

Outside, the garden had eaten the swing set. The oak we planted had grown taller than the roof, indifferent to my going, generous only to the sky.

I stood in the center of all that stillness and understood the terrible arithmetic: a house does not wait for you. A house simply remains, gathering evidence, while you spend yourself elsewhere. It keeps your childhood sealed in dust like a specimen, and when you finally come back to claim it—

the dust is all that's left to hold.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a piece of experimental fiction where a narrator drives back to Zanesville, Ohio, and confronts a house frozen in time, using imagery of dust, snow, and lunar footprints.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Persistence of Snow

The odometer doesn't work anymore, so I measure the drive in songs, in the specific gray of the sky that Ohio manufactures like it's the only export left. Zanesville arrives the way it always does—not as a destination but as a symptom.

*Here is the house.*

I want to tell you it has changed. That would be the merciful fiction. Instead: the house exists in the condition I left it, which is to say the condition of a body in the moment after breath. The porch light is on. The porch light has been on for eleven years. Somewhere a meter is running, counting the cost of my absence in kilowatts.

I park. I do not turn off the engine.

---

Consider dust.

Dust is the democracy of decay, settling equally on the piano my mother couldn't play and the photographs she couldn't stop taking. When I push open the door—unlocked, always unlocked, an invitation extended to no one—the dust hangs suspended in the shaft of light I've introduced. It doesn't fall. It hovers. It has learned patience I never mastered.

Each particle: a former thing. Skin. Cloth. The pulverized cellulose of letters. I am breathing my mother. I am breathing the version of myself that lived here, seventeen and certain the world was elsewhere.

The furniture wears white sheets like a convention of amateur ghosts.

---

Consider snow.

It falls inside the house. This is the part you won't believe, the part I don't believe, and I am *here*, I am watching it accumulate on the kitchen table where we ate in the specific silence of people running out of language. The ceiling is intact. The snow does not care about ceilings. It falls the way memory falls, which is to say: selectively, coldly, covering the sharp edges of what actually happened with something soft and false and beautiful.

I hold out my hand.

The snow lands. Does not melt. My body temperature has become theoretical.

There are footprints in the snow on the kitchen floor. They lead from the table to the back door and they are mine, they are the size of my feet, but the tread is wrong—

---

Consider the moon.

Neil Armstrong was from Ohio. Wapakoneta, ninety minutes west. We learned this in school as though proximity to greatness were itself a kind of achievement, as though the moon were something a boy from Ohio could simply *decide* to reach.

The footprints on the moon are permanent. No wind. No water. No dust to settle because the dust has nowhere to go, no atmosphere to hold it aloft. Armstrong's boot-shape will outlast the memory of the man, outlast the flag, outlast possibly the species that dreamed him upward.

The footprints in my mother's kitchen have that same quality of *permanence*. That same lunar stillness. I place my foot beside them and understand:

I have already been here. In every version. I have always been standing in this snow that doesn't melt, breathing this dust that doesn't fall, in this house that refuses the courtesy of ruin.

---

Here is what confrontation actually looks like:

Not a reckoning. Not a scream. I do not tear the sheets from the furniture. I do not read the letters. I do not play the piano my mother couldn't play, filling the frozen rooms with something like resolution.

I stand in my own footprints.

I fit them perfectly.

Outside, the engine idles, patient as dust, faithful as snow, burning through a fuel that Ohio also once exported, back when the ground here gave things instead of merely holding them.

*Here is the house.*

I am inside it. I have never left it. The drive back to Zanesville is a drive I am always taking, will always be taking, the way light from the moon is always arriving, always four seconds late, always showing you a moon that has already moved on.

The porch light burns.

The meter runs.

The snow falls up, now—reversing, ascending, undoing itself toward a ceiling it never respected—and I follow it with my eyes toward the place where all frozen things are stored, and I think:

*I could stay.*

I think:

*I have stayed.*

The footprints wait for feet that already fill them.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a melancholic, stream-of-consciousness monologue about homecoming, absent fathers, and the strangeness of memory, blending mundane details with dreamlike surrealism.
counterfactuals.output:
The house is smaller than I remembered, or I've grown too large for it, or memory just does that—inflates the rooms of childhood like lungs, then lets them collapse when you finally walk back through the door. The doorknob is the same. Brass, loose, it turns a quarter-inch too far before it catches, and my hand remembers this even though I don't, my hand has been keeping records all these years I never asked it to keep.

There's a smell. Dust and something floral gone stale, potpourri maybe, in a dish, and underneath it the ghost of pipe smoke that can't be real because he's been gone since I was nine, and smells don't wait around for eleven years, do they, they dissipate, they obey physics, but here it is anyway, clinging to the curtains like a thing that refuses.

I keep expecting him at the kitchen table.

That's the strange part, the part I can't explain to anyone—I never really knew him, not enough to miss the actual man, only the shape of where he should have been, a father-shaped absence I carried around like furniture in an empty apartment. But standing in this doorway I expect him, fully, the way you expect the next step on a staircase, that lurch when it isn't there and your whole body drops an inch into nothing.

The wallpaper is peeling in the hall. Yellow roses. I used to trace them when Mom fought with someone on the phone, and now the roses are curling away from the wall like they're trying to leave too, everybody in this house always trying to leave, and I put my finger on one and it's exactly where it was, the same rose, waiting, patient as a photograph.

Did he stand here?

I want to ask the house. Houses know. Houses are just memory with a roof, and this one has held its breath for eleven years and I want to shake it and say tell me, tell me where he stood, tell me if he ever paused in this hallway and thought about the boy asleep upstairs, or if he just walked out clean, no lurch, no dropped inch, just the door and the loose brass knob and then the ordinary miracle of a car starting in the dark.

The clock in the living room is still going. Someone wound it. Mom, before the hospital, her hands doing the last small useful thing, and it ticks now into an empty room like a heart that didn't get the news, and I think: that's grief, isn't it, the machinery that keeps running after the reason stops.

I sit at the table where I expected him.

The chair holds me. The window shows the same backyard, gone to seed, the swing set rusted into a kind of sculpture, orange and reaching, and for a moment—just a moment—the light does something impossible, goes thick and golden and slow, and I'm nine again and he's real again and he's out there pushing me, or I'm dreaming he's pushing me, the two things wearing the same face now, dream and memory, indistinguishable, both of them lying to me gently in the language of the dead.

Higher, I'm saying. Higher.

And the hands on my back could be anyone's.

The light goes normal. The yard is just a yard. The swing set is just rust and the specific loneliness of things built for children who grew up and went away.

I came here to sort through boxes. To be practical. There's a will, there's a lawyer, there's a whole adult apparatus of ending, and instead I'm sitting in a dead woman's kitchen missing a man I invented, in a house that remembers more than I do, and the clock keeps its terrible time, and the roses lean off the wall, and somewhere the pipe smoke curls around nothing.

I'll get up in a minute.

I'll open the first box in a minute.

The doorknob turns a quarter-inch too far and catches, and my hand remembers, and my hand is the only one of us still telling the truth.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a dark, poetic short story that opens with a dead tollbooth keeper and follows a person searching for a home where no one is left.
counterfactuals.output:
The Last Toll

The tollbooth keeper had been dead three days before anyone thought to close his eyes.

I found him upright in his little glass box, one hand still open on the counter as if waiting for coins from travelers who no longer came. The frost had made lace of his eyelashes. His ledger lay open beneath his palm, and every line was blank except the last, where he had written in a shaking hand: *No one passed today. No one passes anymore.*

I put two pennies over his eyes—not for the ferryman, but because it seemed cruel to leave him staring at a road that had forgotten how to carry the living. Then I lifted the wooden arm of his gate, which he had lowered against nothing, and I walked through into the country beyond.

I was looking for home. I should tell you that now, before the road gets long.

Not *my* home—that had burned or drowned or simply grown over, I no longer remembered which. I was looking for *a* home, any home, a place where a door might still hang on its hinges and a hearth might remember warmth. I had heard, in the way one hears things in the dark, that such a place waited at the end of this road. A house where no one was left. A house that had been swept clean of grief because it had run out of people to grieve.

That was what I wanted. Not company. Company dies. I wanted the quiet that comes *after*.

---

The first village was a mouth full of broken teeth.

The houses leaned toward one another like old men sharing secrets, and the wind moved through them making a sound almost like conversation. I went from door to door. In one, a table was set for supper, the plates furred green, the chairs pushed out as though everyone had risen at once and simply decided not to return. In another, a cradle rocked in a draft that came from nowhere.

"Is anyone home?" I called, and the houses answered with the small settling sounds that empty things make—the tick of cooling wood, the sigh of a beam giving up another inch of its long surrender.

But it was not empty enough. I could feel them there, the ones who had left. Their absence had a shape, and the shape was still warm. This was not a place where no one was left. This was a place where everyone had *just* gone, and the going still ached in the walls like a pulled tooth.

I could not live in another person's fresh wound.

I walked on.

---

The road climbed. The trees thinned into black staves against a sky the color of a drowned man's lips. I passed a church with its bell rope still swinging, though no hand held it and no wind was strong enough. I passed a well, and when I looked down, I saw my own face very far below, older than I remembered, mouthing words I could not hear.

I began to understand something about the place I was looking for.

A house where no one is left is not a house where people have died. Death leaves too much behind—the imprint of a body on a mattress, the last thought hanging in the air of a room. No. A house where no one is left is a house that has been *unremembered*. A house no living mind still holds. When the last person who ever thought of a place stops thinking, the place comes loose from the world, drifts free, and goes to wait at the end of the road for someone like me.

I was looking for a house that even the dead had forgotten.

---

I found her at the crossroads, an old woman with a lantern that gave no light.

"You're the one walking to the end," she said. It was not a question.

"I'm looking for a home."

"I know what you're looking for." She lifted the dark lantern and studied me by the absence it cast. "You want the house where no one's left. But child, do you know what makes a house that way?"

"Time," I said. "Loss. The slow subtraction of everyone."

She laughed, and it was the sound of the tollbooth keeper's ledger closing. "No. A house becomes that way when the *last one out* is the one who wanted only to be alone. When the last heart in it turned from the door and said, *let no one follow, let no one remember, let this place forget it ever held a light.* That is the wish that unhouses a house. That is the toll." She leaned close. "You've paid it already. You've been paying it your whole life."

I did not answer her. There was nothing in me that could.

---

The house was there when I crested the final hill, and I knew it the way you know your own reflection in black water—not with joy, but with a terrible recognition.

It was small. Its windows were dark, but not with emptiness. They were dark the way an eye is dark that has decided to see nothing more. The door hung open. No smoke rose. No absence warmed the walls, because no one had ever loved this house enough to leave a wound in it. It was clean. It was quiet. It was the silence that comes *after*, exactly as I had wished.

I understood then whose house it was.

I had built it myself, in every room I ever walked out of. In every hand I let go of before it could let go of me. In every home I fled because staying meant one day being the one left behind. I had wished my whole life to arrive somewhere no grief could follow, and the world, patient as a tollkeeper, had kept my ledger and built me exactly what I asked for.

A house where no one is left.

I stepped inside. The door did not close behind me; there was no wind, no hand, no one to close it. There never would be. That was the point. That had always been the point.

I sat down at the cold hearth in the perfect quiet I had spent a lifetime earning, and I finally understood the tollbooth keeper's last words—not as an epitaph, but as a welcome.

*No one passes anymore.*

I put two pennies on the mantel, for the next one who comes looking. There is always a next one. We are a long road, we who cannot bear to be the ones left behind, and we walk it single file, each of us certain we are the only one, each of us arriving at the same empty house to discover that solitude, when you finally reach it, has a door but no lock—

because nothing that is already alone

has anything left to keep out.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a literary passage in the style of a contemporary American poet about time, dust settling over everything, and the impossibility of ever really coming home.
counterfactuals.output:
# What the Dust Remembers

There is a house I keep returning to
that no longer exists—or exists
only in the particular slant of four o'clock,
the way light lies down on the floorboards
like something exhausted, something
that has walked a great distance to get here.

Dust is only time made visible.
This is what my mother never told me,
sweeping it from the sills each morning
as if she could keep the hours
from accumulating on our lives,
as if the past were something
you could simply refuse.

But it settles anyway. On the piano
no one plays. On the photographs
where we are always younger,
always squinting into a sun
that has long since moved on
to warm some other country.

I have tried to come home.
I have driven the old roads at dusk,
past the fields gone to seed,
past the water tower with its faded name,
and found only the shape of longing
where the thing itself should be.

Because home is not a place—
I know this now—but a moment
you cannot re-enter,
a room the self has already left,
turning off the light behind it,
pulling the door soft against the frame.

What remains is this:
the fine gray sediment of years,
the way it gathers in the corners
of everything we meant to keep.
Run your finger through it.
See how it rises, briefly,
into the light—
and then, like all of us,
comes down.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
